topic_name: Rationale for a Dedicated Reports Service

voiceover_data.topic_name: Rationale for a Dedicated Reports Service

voice_over.title: Transactional vs. Analytical Split
voice_over.narration: Building on how our reporting layer leverages shared foundations, we face a design question. Why build a dedicated Reports Service instead of just adding report endpoints to our existing services? Our current services are built for online transaction processing, or O L T P. Think of this as day-to-day work optimized for fast, single-row actions like booking a class. These represent our hot path, the high-frequency route that we must keep fast and responsive at all times. Reporting is different. It is online analytical processing, or O L A P: heavy queries that scan and total up thousands of records. In G M S these queries still run against the same shared MySQL database, but running them in their own service keeps them from tying up the workers that serve bookings and check-ins. The key idea is to keep transactional tasks separate from analytical ones.

voice_over.title: Solving the Dependency Knot
voice_over.narration: Now that we have separated those needs, let us look at why a separate service solves the dependency problem between our domains. Consider an attendance report. It needs data from both member profiles and class bookings. If we added it to the member service, that service would have to reach into class and booking data that belongs to another domain, causing tight coupling. A dedicated Reports Service, which summarizes metrics without owning any state of its own, avoids this by keeping all reporting requirements in one place. By sitting above the other services, it reads the shared tables directly, so the member and class services never have to call each other just to build a report. Memory anchor: separate services prevent messy cross-domain dependencies. Keeping report queries in one place means no domain service has to carry another domain's logic.

voice_over.title: Focused Optimization and Scaling
voice_over.narration: Moving beyond structure, let us discuss how this isolation allows us to optimize reporting without hurting our transactional services. Isolation lets us tune reporting on its own terms. We can rewrite report queries, change how results are grouped, or give the service more workers without touching the booking or payment code. Indexes are a different story: because G M S uses one shared database, an index added for a report must also be maintained on every write, so it has to be weighed against the transactional side. This independence also helps with growth. The Reports Service runs in its own container with its own pool of web workers, so when report demand spikes we can scale that service alone. The shared database is still a common resource, which is why later lessons look at offloading reads. Memory anchor: isolate services to tune their unique resource needs.

voice_over.title: Architectural Trade-offs
voice_over.narration: Finally, we must weigh these benefits against the costs of managing an additional service within the G M S architecture. A separate service adds infrastructure overhead: one more container to build, deploy, and monitor. Some systems also offload reporting to a read replica, a read-only copy of the database, but G M S does not use one. Reports read the same live database as everything else, so there is no second copy to keep in sync. We accept the overhead of a dedicated service to preserve clear boundaries and keep our system clean. By choosing this path, we prioritize long-term system health over initial simplicity. Memory anchor: trade complexity today for a more scalable tomorrow. We accept slight operational overhead to gain long-term architectural clarity. Now that we understand why reporting gets a service of its own, we can look at its front door: how the report endpoint is designed.
